tagline.text: An underground adventure from Lumiang Cave to Sumaguing Cave

location.label: Location
location.text: South Road around Sumaguing Cave, Sagada, Mountain Province

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,500 (guide, shuttle and registration for a group of 4)

children.text: This 3–5 hour route takes you into Lumiang Cave in Sagada, through rock scrambles, tight squeezes and cold pools, and out through Sumaguing Cave. You get both the limestone scenery and the atmosphere of an old burial cave.
Sagada is a highland mountain town at about

above sea level, and its cool climate and relaxed pace have long made it popular with travelers. Limestone caves cluster along the South Road on the south side of town, and the best-known route among them is the "Cave Connection," which links Lumiang Cave to Sumaguing Cave.

The two caves are known to belong to the same cave system, so you can enter through one and exit through the other. The Lumiang entrance is reached down a flight of concrete steps, and old wooden coffins are stacked near the mouth. Sagada is known for its tradition of placing coffins in caves and on cliffs, and the custom continues today, so please treat the coffins as someone's grave, not as a sight to photograph.

From the Lumiang side, the route runs through a section of climbing down big boulders, narrow gaps that fit one person at a time, a pitch-dark stretch where you can hear bats overhead, and then the wet limestone and stalactite-and-stalagmite section on the Sumaguing side. Some spots have safety ropes, but you still need real arm and leg strength to brace yourself. Once you are inside it is hard to turn back, so check your fitness and any claustrophobia beforehand.

This entry covers the longer and harder connection route, not the standard half-day Sumaguing Cave out-and-back. A guide is mandatory, registration and guide assignment happen at the local tourist office, and the route can be suspended depending on weather and water levels. Fees and procedures change often, so check the latest announcements before you go.

blocks.title: Lumiang Cave entrance and old coffins

children.text: Down the concrete steps, wooden coffins lie near the cave mouth. They are a glimpse of Sagada's long-standing burial culture, so please do not touch them or use them as photo props, and pass quietly.

In the Lumiang section you climb down big rocks using your hands and feet, and some gaps allow only one person at a time. A few difficult spots have safety ropes, but you still need your own strength.
Some stretches are so dark that you see nothing when the lights go off, and you can hear bats overhead. You move by the light of the guide's gas lamp and your headlamp.

The closer you get to Sumaguing, the wetter and slipperier the floor becomes, and stalactites and stalagmites of all sizes appear. They are formed as limestone slowly dissolves and is redeposited by water, so do not touch them.
The water in the cave pools is very cold, and its depth varies a lot with recent rain. It can reach from ankle to knee height or more, so enter only when your guide tells you to cross.
On wet limestone, bare feet often grip better than shoes, so guides sometimes suggest going barefoot. A pair of sandals is easy to put on and take off.
Your Sagada guide explains the cave's layout and place names, the burial culture and how to place your feet safely. As you walk, you see why no one enters without a guide.

items.title: Same-day afternoon route
items.subtitle: From registration to the connection route

children.text: Register as a visitor at the Sagada tourist information office and pay
. If you registered online in advance, you can skip the line. Get your Cave Connection guide assigned and ask about the cave's condition that day.
Eat a light lunch, since a full stomach makes tight squeezes harder. Pack water, snacks, a waterproof bag and a dry change of clothes.
Travel to the Lumiang cave entrance by shuttle or local vehicle. You can walk from town, but the shuttle saves time for the route.
Listen to the guide's safety briefing and descend into Lumiang. You pass the boulder section, the tight squeezes and the dark stretch on your way toward Sumaguing.
Pass the pools and the stalagmite zone in the Sumaguing section and exit the cave. Some sources say the last entry is around 4 PM, but this varies by day, so confirm locally.
Back at your lodging, wash up and have something warm to eat. Dry your wet shoes and clothes well.
These times are examples and change with cave conditions and group pace. Starting early in the morning gives you more room, and on days when rain is forecast it is safer to postpone.

items.title: Two-day Sagada route
items.subtitle: Combining the cave with the town's scenery

children.text: Arrive in Sagada by bus from Baguio or Manila, drop your bags at your lodging and have breakfast.
Register at the tourist office, then tour Echo Valley and the Hanging Coffins with a guide. A separate entrance fee of about
is reported there.
Start the Cave Connection. If you have other plans on another day, doing it in the morning is easier on your body.
Have dinner at a restaurant in town and rest early. Sagada gets quite cool after sunset.
The next morning, consider a light activity such as sunrise and sea-of-clouds trekking at Marlboro Hills. Your legs will be sore after the cave, so avoid anything strenuous.
A Coda Lines overnight bus from Cubao, Quezon City, runs directly to Sagada and takes about
12–13 hours
. Departures are usually in the evening, between 8 and 11 PM.
Fares range from about ₱760 to ₱1,200 depending on seat class and season, and sources differ, so confirm when you book.
Book through Coda Lines by phone or email, or through an online booking site. In peak season it is better to buy tickets ahead.
According to Sagada tourism information, GL Trans tickets can only be bought in person. Schedules can change, so check the latest announcements.
Travel from Manila to Baguio by Victory Liner or similar, then take a Sagada-bound bus from the GL Trans terminal in Baguio.
Baguio to Sagada takes about
4–6 hours
and costs about ₱220–450, depending on the source. Some sources say the last bus leaves around 1 PM, so start early in the morning.
The GL Trans schedule in the tourism information lists several departures between
in the early morning and
in the afternoon, but confirm actual service locally.
From Banaue to Sagada, a jeepney or van takes about
3 hours
and costs roughly ₱400–700. Vans sometimes leave only when a minimum number of passengers is reached.
Bontoc is about
18km
from Sagada and is served by jeepneys.
Take the tourist shuttle from the Sagada tourist information office, walk or use a local vehicle. Many sources list the shuttle at around
(per group).
Some lodgings offer the shuttle free to their guests.
You are advised to leave visitor vehicles at your lodging and use the tourist shuttle.
Sagada is cool all year, and according to Wikipedia the average annual daily high is about
and the low about
. February is the coldest month at an average of about
, and annual rainfall is about 2,835 mm, most of it between May and October.

Underground water can rise suddenly even from rain that falls elsewhere. In the rainy season caves are often closed and the connection route is frequently suspended, so the dry season from November to May is safer and your plans are more likely to work out. Even if you planned a month ahead, check the route's status at the tourist office the day before.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Cave conditions are the most stable. Bring warm clothes, because you get cold when you come out wet.
Peak season with many visitors. During the Etag Festival in late February, lodgings fill up quickly.
Water levels rise and the route is sometimes suspended, and landslides can block roads.

and may vary depending on local conditions.

Sagada has many guesthouses and homestays in and around the town center, typically ₱350–600 per person per night. Some lodges provide the shuttle free of charge, so ask when you book. Book early for the Etag Festival in late February.

Cafés such as Yoghurt House, Gaia Cafe and Sagada Brew are well known and good for resting after the cave. A meal is typically about ₱200–250, and Sagada is known for coffee, local vegetable dishes and yogurt. Eat lightly before the cave and have a hot soup or a proper meal afterward.
Always confirm the cave's condition that day, whether the Cave Connection is running, any group size limit and the latest fees at the tourist information office.
Registering in advance on the online registration site (umali-kayo.sagada.gov.ph) can shorten the line on arrival.
Wear quick-dry clothes and sandals or shoes with good grip, and avoid jeans and flip-flops.
Keep valuables in a waterproof bag, and bring or leave at your lodging a dry change of clothes, a towel and spare socks.
A personal headlamp as a backup gives peace of mind if the guide's light moves ahead.
Use a waterproof case for your camera and ask your guide before you shoot.
The larger the group, the slower the movement, so split into small groups of 3–4 if you can.
Your legs will ache after the cave, so keep the next day light.

The connection route is longer and harder than the standard Sumaguing route, with tight gaps, darkness and cold water throughout. If you have weak knees or back, claustrophobia, or small children, choose the standard Sumaguing course or another activity.
A guide is mandatory. Do not follow offers from anyone other than a registered guide.
Wet limestone is very slippery. Keep three points of contact (two hands and one foot, or one hand and two feet) and do not stand beneath someone who is climbing.
Sound echoes in the cave and it is easy to lose your group. Do not follow another group's light, and stay close to your guide.
Do not touch coffins, stalagmites or stones, take them away or carve names. Do not use soap in the pools.
If it is raining or there was heavy rain just before, water levels can rise sharply, so postpone. Operations can be suspended without notice.
Echo Valley, the Hanging Coffins, Marlboro Hills, waterfalls and other sights reachable on foot or by shuttle are clustered here. The town is about
2km
away.
This highland city, where Sagada-bound buses depart, is a good overnight stop on the way from Manila. It is about
4–6 hours
from Sagada.
About
3 hours
from Sagada by jeepney or van, it can be added to a northern Cordillera itinerary.
Luzon's second-highest peak, popular for sunrise treks, reached from the Baguio and Kabayan side.
